Everyone’s obsessed with what’s next for Paul Seixas, but shouldn’t we be thinking more about Primož Roglič ?

The modern era’s grand tour OG is out of contract with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and he’s running out of time to secure his future.

Having been linked to seemingly half the teams in the pro peloton , Roglič’s options are becoming increasingly thin.

According to contract super-sleuth Daniel Benson, a previously muted link up with Tom Pidcock at Pinarello-Q36.5 is now off the table. Benson reported the news Wednesday on Twitter / X .

If correct, that will be another team crossed off the list of options for a rider who clearly has more to give.

Roglič dogged out second place at the Vuelta a España in September before he bounded to an unforeseen European time trial title one month later.

Despite Roglič’s late-season resurgence and his ongoing will to race into 2027, he’s accepted his days might be numbered.

“You never know when is the last [race],” Roglič said last month before he finished 10th at Il Lombardia.

When pressed on whether he will continue to race next year, Roglič said, “I don’t know yet. We will see. We will see.”

Benson’s reporting on Wednesday makes it seem increasingly likely that “The Race of the Falling Leaves” was Roglič’s last dance, whether he likes it or not.

“What’s next for Roglič” has become a saga worthy of its own Box Set.

He was linked to Lotto-Intermarché way back in summer but reportedly turned down the Belgian team’s offer.

Since then, the five-time grand tour winner has variously been connected to Unibet Rose Rockets, Tudor Pro Cycling, and his former team, Visma-Lease a Bike.

Het Laatste Nieuws reported last week that initial talks between Roglič and Visma have been called off.

Unibet Rose Rockets founder Bas Tietema revealed he had contact with Roglič ahead of the Vuelta a España, but made no suggestion of intent.

And the chances of a move to Tudor are looking increasingly slim – though Fabian Cancellara’s ambitious young team does still have a space on its roster.

With Pinarello-Q36.5 seemingly out of the running, Roglič’s time – and options – are running out.

Roglič may be without a contract for next year, but the four-time Vuelta a España champion and Giro d’Italia winner still holds some star power.

The Slovenian will do the rounds as a special guest at the Taiwan Masters Ride on Monday, November 9.

He and a selection of B-tier pros will be joined by a mob of local fans in a ride outside of Taipei.

But who knows, that could be Roglič’s last ride as a pro.

It would be a strange way to bow out for a rider who’s been so definitive of the modern era.

Having turned 37 just last week, Rogla is one of the few survivors of the pre-pandemic age – a time of rim brakes and 175mm cranks – to have remained competitive in his craft.

The riders who finished behind “the Slovenian who was a ski jumper” when he claimed his first Vuelta a España victory in 2019 reads like a pro cycling retirement home. Tadej Pogačar, then in his grand tour debut , is the one anomaly alongside Alejandro Valverde, Nairo Quintana, Rafal Majka, and the disgraced “superman” López.

In the seven years since Vuelta win No.1, Roglič has become the peloton’s enduring enigma, a rider who either crashes or crushes, and who says everything and nothing all at once.

With 93 wins on his palmarès, he’s one of the most celebrated riders in the bunch. Pogačar is the only active pro to have won more.

Roglič is far from his peak. With only two wins in 2026, this was the least successful year of his pro career.

But he’s refused to be pushed out of the picture altogether.

His defiant home victory at Ljubljana’s European time trial championships proves that point.

“It’s beautiful, it’s of course for me, but it’s also for all the people,” Roglič said after he accepted the white-and-blue Euro jersey.

“My radio stopped working. It cut out in the first kilometer of the race, so I was completely lost,” he added. “I just went with my instincts.”

Roglič’s European TT victory was as unlikely as it gets.

He might need to pull something equally unlikely to be able to wear that champion’s jersey in 2027.

Wout van Aert’s emotional victory at Paris-Roubaix. Demi Vollering’s rout of road worlds. Tadej Pogačar’s crash ‘n’ comeback conquest of Milan-San Remo.

The 2026 cycling season was loaded with races for the ages.

It was sprinkled with plenty of controversies, catastrophes, and meme-worthy WTFs, too.

Remember Mathieu van der Poel’s pedal fiasco at Paris-Roubaix?

Or the beef-to-end-all-beefs between Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney at the Tour de France Femmes?

And there’s surely no forgetting Jonas Vingegaard’s dungaree-inspired solution to keeping toasty at Paris-Nice.

We’ve rewound through the bike-racing bloopers of 2026 to select the wildest, wackiest moments of the season. Strap in for a recap of mechanical meltdowns, dubious maneuvers, and some debate about “bra doping.”

One of the most hotly debated, sensationally divisive moments of this cycling season occurred away from the damning proof of TV cameras.

The Tour de France Femmes exploded into the biggest beef in recent memory when something happened between Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and Demi Vollering’s superdomestique Célia Gery on stage 8 of the race.

Riding at the front of the pack, Gery, Vollering, and Niewiadoma blasted into a tight left-hand corner at the entrance to a decisive kicker climb.

Broadcast footage cuts from an overhead drone shot as the bunch dives under tree cover, and returns to a front-on moto camera shot a split second later.

The race tilted on its head in that one unseen moment.

According to Niewiadoma, Gery took her out of Vollering’s wheels as the Dutchwoman attacked. Niewiadoma was unable to respond and was blown out of the yellow jersey by the end of the stage.

“Gery on purpose just blocked me to the barriers where I had to stop pedaling,” Niewiadoma claimed.

“If they want to compete, they should compete fair play and not look for me to close me in the barriers,” Niewiadoma said. “I feel like it’s so childish.”

UCI commissaires had nothing to say. The cycling world was left attempting to piece together fragmented fan footage to figure it out.

Social media duly blew up with speculation and armchair sleuthing.

Gery was blasted by online death threats.

The final stage of the Femmes played out in the shadow of a volatile, bubbling beef between eternal rivals Niewiadoma and Vollering.

The two superstar riders attempted to turn down the volume on the controversy ahead of Vollering’s crowning stage 9 victory, but by then it was too late.

“Kasia Corner” had launched the Femmes beyond cycling media and onto the world stage.

Alpecin-Premier Tech showed the peloton how not to win Paris-Roubaix with smart tech choices this year.

Mathieu van der Poel and Jasper Philipsen threw away their podium chances in a meme-worthy cleat kerfuffle on the kingmaker cobbles of the Trouée d’Arenberg.

When three-time Roubaix champion MVDP punctured on the notorious stones, Philipsen selflessly handed his wingman his bike.

Philipsen was riding a prototype of Shimano’s new cleat-pedal system. Van der Poel and the rest of the team were rocking the standard-issue, outgoing set-up.

The two aren’t compatible , as MVDP was about to find out.

Clearly unaware of the mismatch, Van der Poel hopped onto Philipsen’s bike and optimistically pushed off onto the cobbles. After a few foiled attempts to clip in, the cobblestone crusher tossed aside the useless bike and walked forlornly back down the verge in hope of some help.

Meanwhile, Alpecin-Premier Tech’s Tibor del Grosso had been busy swapping an inflated wheel from his bike to Van der Poel’s original, discarded ride.

More than two minutes after his puncture, Van der Poel was back on a bike with two inflated tires, a pedal system that suited his cleats, and was chasing hard.

Any hope of a comeback didn’t last long. A few hundred meters later, Van der Poel flatted again.

Team boss Christoph Roodhooft stepped up after the race to cop the blame.

“Of course, that came together at an incredibly bad time. I never thought it would happen,” Roodhooft told Sporza . “We made the decision to use the pedals in race conditions.

“I never thought it would come together like this,” he said. “It is what it is. It won’t happen again, but it’s over now.”

Philipsen dutifully praised his team sponsor’s new shoes on Instagram when they officially launched this September.

“Finally, I can show you what I’ve been racing on all season. The new S-Phyre RC910 shoes and Dura-Ace PD-R9300 pedals,” Philipsen wrote alongside a Shimano promo reel.

“I’m proud to have played a part in their development.”

We wonder what Van der Poel thinks of them.

The only way to beat Demi Vollering in 2026 was to pray she took a wrong turn.

Vollering’s Hall of Fame season suffered its only blip this March when she and a whole horde of favorites took a wrong turn in the high-stakes denouement of Strade Bianche.

An attack group was around one minute up the road.

Only 33km remained to the iconic finale on the Piazza del Campo.

Vollering, Lotte Kopecky, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, and Anna van der Breggen were in a small chase group with no time to lose.

Unfortunately, they all lost a lot of time when they mistakenly followed a race moto off course down a side track strewn with rocky boulders.

Vollering and Co. rattled down the stony path for a few hundred meters before realizing this was a level of sterrato far too extreme for Tuscany’s white-roads classic.

They pulled to a halt, awkwardly unclipped, waddled their bikes around a full 180, and returned to the race course. But by then, there was no coming back. They were three minutes behind the leaders and without hope.

Who was to blame for the off-course chaos? The moto or the riders?

The driver no doubt made a mistake, but riders are required to know the course.

Kopecky later admitted herd mentality prevailed in the heat of the chase.…

Will Vingegaard return to the Giro or bet everything on the Tour? (Photo: Getty Images)

The Giro d’Italia just gave Jonas Vingegaard plenty of reasons to return in 2027 with a route that keeps pointing uphill.

A mountain time trial, the Mortirolo and Gavia, and a penultimate showdown on Monte Zoncolan serve up the defending champion a near-perfect course to defend pink as Visma-Lease a Bike maps out his return from a season-ending crash.

The Tour de France ? Some are calling it the Anti-Pogačar Tour , but in many ways, it looks even less inviting for Vingo.

With just three summit finishes and 71km of individual time trialing, the 2027 Tour offers fewer chances for the Dane to turn the screws with his Pogi-killer climbing power that delivered his two yellow jerseys.

So heading into the winter team camps, Visma and Vingegaard face a season-deciding quandary.

Would another run at pink give him a better chance of winning a grand tour in 2027 before another July clash with Tadej Pogačar ?

Or would another Giro take too much out of him and leave him empty in his pursuit of yellow?

The urgent question facing the Visma brain-trust now is how to win another grand tour while also giving Vingegaard his best shot at beating Pogačar.

Vingegaard is being squeezed from all directions as the 2026 season is a wrap.

He’ll be 30 in December, Pogačar remains his bête noire , and a new generation of GC riders is nipping at his heels.

King Pog keeps raising the bar in front of him, and after signing a blockbuster contract extension , he isn’t going anywhere. Behind him, Remco Evenepoel , Isaac del Toro, and Paul Seixas are pumping new hype and ambition into the grand tour conversation.

The Dane who twice beat Pogačar at the Tour now finds himself defending his place as the Slovenian’s most dangerous rival.

Vingegaard boasts four grand tour victories, yet some are already writing him off as the best candidate to crack the Pogačar code.

That’s a strange place to be for someone who ran away with the pink jersey just a few months ago.

And it puts huge pressure on Visma and Vingegaard for the choices they have to make for 2027.

Another pink jersey would underline how good he still is. A third yellow would silence those already writing him off.

So far, neither Vingegaard nor his team is giving much away.

Visma’s official reaction Tuesday to the Giro route offered zero clues. Head of racing Marc Reef praised the course without revealing the team’s plans for 2027.

“To win this Giro d’Italia, you need to have a wide range of qualities. That makes it a really exciting challenge,” Reef said. “We will study the route carefully before putting together the best possible plan.”

This year, Visma and Vingegaard took plenty of heat for attempting the Giro-Tour double.

The first part worked like a charm, with Vingegaard riding away with pink to complete the grand tour sweep.

The Tour went off the rails when he gave up time to Pogačar in the first week and then crashed out on stage 15 with a broken clavicle. He hasn’t raced since.

Team boss Richard Plugge told TV2 after the Tour reveal last month that the yellow jersey remains the central goal for the Killer Bees.

Whether a Giro defense fits into that calculation remains the big question.

Never one to go over the top on social media or give too many interviews, Vingo is leaving everyone guessing about his grand tour plans. No decisions have been announced.

Vingo remains the only rider to beat Pogačar at the Tour, winning in 2022 and 2023. Since then, the Slovenian has been unstoppable with three straight yellow jerseys, but Vingegaard has never given up.

Yet some are already suggesting that he will have a hard time even hitting the Tour podium in 2027 on a course that, on paper, doesn’t favor his strengths.

Ex-pro Michael Rasmussen believes the time trial-heavy, summit-light Tour route reflects the evolving hierarchy inside the elite men’s peloton.

“I don’t think ASO still sees Vingegaard as Pogačar’s main challenger,” Rasmussen said on Viaplay . “I see more potential in the riders coming up behind him.”

Yet fewer summit finishes don’t mean Vingegaard won’t a fighting chance for yellow.

He’s not that bad at time trialing, and the Tour still includes a late showdown on Col du Portet featuring the Tourmalet and 5,400m of climbing. That’s Vingegaard’s happy place.

And who could have guessed Pogačar would have crashed out of the Vuelta a España?

Visma remains one of the most successful teams of the decade, with grand tour victories hard-wired into its DNA. It won’t give up on yellow easily.

The ultimate question for Vingegaard and Visma is what matters more: winning another Giro or going all in for a third yellow jersey?

That could make for a few sleepless nights inside the Visma bus.

There’s another wrinkle: This year’s Giro-Tour bet ended without a clear resolution for the brain-trust inside the Visma bus.

Visma won the opening team time trial in Barcelona, but Vingegaard steadily lost time and then crashed out two weeks later at the foot of the Alps. And even though he was already four minutes-plus behind Pogačar, the team’s data wizards never got the final week of racing to complete their assessment.

Missing from much of this discussion is Vingegaard himself.

The last official team update came on August 17, when Visma confirmed Vingegaard wouldn’t race again this year. Since then, it’s been crickets and his 2027 program remains under wraps.

It’s hard to imagine Vingo not racing the Tour.

He’s Visma’s marquee grand tour leader, and winning the yellow jersey remains the assignment. And King Pog already confirmed where he will be in July.

Would going back to the Giro be read as waving the white flag for July? Some will inevitably see it that way.

But betting everything on the Tour and coming back empty-handed carries its own risk.

Repeating the double in 2027 would come with the same risk and potential reward.…

UAE's Matxin is dreaming big for 2027 despite a crash-filled season. (Photo: Getty Images)

UAE Emirates-XRG endured 78 crashes and fractures to more than half its roster, including world No. 1 Tadej Pogačar , in a season of unprecedented carnage for cycling’s super team in 2026.

UAE’s response? Team boss Joxean Fernández “Matxin” wants an even stronger Pogačar and a clean sweep of cycling’s three grand tours.

Pogačar’s season-ending Vuelta a España crash was the biggest blow in an injury-ravaged campaign that still produced 78 victories from 20 riders despite a season filled with spills, injuries, and broken bones.

“This year we’ve had very bad luck with crashes. We’ve had 78 crashes. Eighteen of our 30 riders have suffered fractures,” Matxin told Eurosport . “I think all those circumstances have made us strong and pushed us to surpass ourselves.”

By Matxin’s count, those 78 wins came with 78 crashes, meaning that UAE’s season produced as many victories as wipeouts, with fractures affecting more than half its roster.

Despite the endless wave of crashes, the team still ended 2026 ranked No. 1 in the world and won more races than any squad in the WorldTour.

That’s well off its record haul of 97 wins in 2025, however, showing just how devastating crashes were across cycling’s richest team.

Even after the bruising season, Matxin is raising the bar for 2027 with the ambition of winning the Giro d’Italia, Tour de France, and Vuelta in the same season.

“What am I longing for right now? I won’t lie to you: what Visma achieved, winning the Giro, Tour and Vuelta in the same year,” he said.

That assumes a healthy Pogačar is back in 2027 and the team can avoid a repeat of the costly spills.

Things were worse behind the scenes than many realized.

Matxin also revealed how UAE team doctor Adrian Rotunno pumped the brakes on Pogačar’s return to racing this fall.

The Slovenian initially hoped to return for the European championships after his devastating Vuelta crash.

Rotunno and the team’s medical staff were firm in advising that his racing season was over, and Matxin now credits them with making the right call.

“The medical team, led by Adrian Rotunno, was very firm in advising that his year was over,” Matxin told Eurosport .

“On the sporting side, you’re always thinking about whether he can make it back, whether he can win,” he said. “But the medical team’s clear-headed approach determined that the best thing was to end his season so we wouldn’t take any risks.”

Pogačar was champing at the bit to return to racing on the Euros on home roads in Slovenia just weeks after he crashed out of the Spanish grand tour, but later scans proved that ending his season and focusing on recovery was the prudent call.

“I think it was a wise decision and I have to thank them for it, because from my sporting perspective, you’re probably always looking at when he can return and be available,” Matxin said.

Pogačar is now training on open roads and looks to be on track for a full recovery.

But Pogačar’s own account underlines how bad things were. The Slovenian revealed to The Athletic last week that further scans uncovered two additional fractured vertebrae after his August 29 Vuelta crash.

“When I saw I had three broken vertebrae? I’m just happy to be alive, actually, or just to be standing,” he told The Athletic .

Matxin now sees the forced stop only fueling King Pog’s ambitions for 2027 .

“I have no doubt that Pogačar will be better than last year,” Matxin said.

There is some speculation that Pogačar could be a different rider after the high-speed Vuelta crash, but Matxin said he doesn’t expect him to lose any of his winning edge in the aftermath of the Slovenian’s first major injury.

“When you go through difficult moments and suffer, you savor the good moments more and make more of them,” he said. “I think you have to take something positive from everything in life, and in the bad moments you have to know that you’re going to come back stronger, with that little bit of anger that helps you improve.”

Matxin also brushed aside the idea of focusing solely on breakout French star Paul Seixas as Pogačar’s biggest Tour threat .

“You can’t rule out Remco. You can’t rule out Jonas. And obviously you can’t rule out Paul Seixas, because he has made such a brilliant breakthrough,” he said.

As for suggestions of an “anti-Pogačar” Tour route , Matxin understands why organizers want to keep the fight for yellow alive.

“What the organizers are looking for, and I understand them here, is to make sure the Tour isn’t decided by the fourth stage,” he said. “I understand that perspective.”

Matxin didn’t reveal any firm calendars yet for 2027, but if the grand tour sweep is on the radar, that would suggest that Isaac del Toro could head to the Giro d’Italia while Pogačar might repeat the Tour-Vuelta double.

There’s also talk that he might skip Paris-Roubaix, and emphasis on knocking off a record sixth yellow jersey and a first Vuelta to complete the grand tour sweep.

Those details will be sorted in the coming weeks at the team’s winter camps in Spain in December.

Nothing screams “off-season” more than when pro cyclists start popping crazy running performances into your Strava feed.

Whether it’s Mathieu van der Poel blasting 10Ks while nose-breathing or Andreas Leknessund and Alexys Brunel obliterating half- and full-marathon races, the ride-to-run pivot is as seasonal as pumpkin-flavored everything .

But if you’re feeling inspired to do the same now the fondo season is over and the weather is turning grim, don’t lace up your runners just yet.

An overzealous new running regimen could leave you with DOMS so bad you’ve got to walk down stairs backward and might not be any benefit when you’re back on the bike.

There’s a reason why Tom Dumoulin waited to retire before he clipped off a sub-2:30 at the New York Marathon .

And even for the most experienced runners, the crossover benefit to cycling is still unproven. A marathon P.B. in winter won’t guarantee an FTP personal best in spring.

But what about the benefits for bone health? We hear your cries. Well, some pro trainers have thoughts on that, too.

Here’s what cyclists should know before they take up running this off-season.

We cover what the pros do, the risks and benefits for you, and how to start running without smashing your capacity to cycle.

“Pro cyclist does stupid-fast run” is like a meme that’s auto-posted every autumn.

Riders driven stir-crazy by weeks without structure, competition, and a mandate to stay away from the bike often lace up their trainers at this time of year for an annoyingly fast “jog.”

Adam Yates, Tom Pidcock, and Tiffany Cromwell are among the active pros who’ve laced rapid running performances in off-seasons past.

This year, Brunel of TotalEnergies and Leknessund of Uno-X Mobility stepped up to stoke the annual “cyclist runs fast” meme.

Brunel finished 20th at the Lille Marathon in a smokin’ fast time of 2:26 . Leknessund casually ran a 1:15 at the Amsterdam Half Marathon, despite having run little more than 100km in the past year.

Those are times even the most devoted enthusiast runner would lose all their toenails and get plantar fasciitis for.

Brunel and Leknessund’s cycling coaches might not have been so impressed.

Tudor Pro Cycling performance guru James Spragg told Velo that even the strongest pros tread a tightrope if they pivot to running too fast.

“Those guys can run very good times compared to regular runners because they’ve got that huge cardiovascular base. But they don’t have the mechanical adaptations, and that makes them very average against a world-class runner. And that’s also where the injury risk can come up,” Spragg said.

“Cyclists who suddenly cross over don’t have the shock resistance that’s built in the cartilage over time, or the tendon stiffness which gives you running efficiency. They are mechanical adaptations that you need to get from running,” Spragg said.

“Trying to go too far or too fast without those can be dangerous.”

Brunel and Leknessund appear to have built some running base before they blasted their recent races. Their injury risks might not have been extreme.

Riders who feel inspired to start running fall into a trap of pushing harder than their bodies, pampered by years of non-weight-bearing sport, can handle.

“The one thing we as coaches have in our ‘advantage’ with cyclists coming into running is normally they do one run, and then the DOMS protects them from themselves,” Spragg laughed.

“They run once and then don’t run again until the next off-season.”

Pros “have” to step away from the bike in autumn to reset themselves for the next season of self-flagellation.

Amateur riders don’t have 10 months of heinous workouts and 50kph racing to steel themselves for, but there’s a similar temptation to take a winter break.

Short, dank days, and the end of a season of fondos, races, and adventures can make bike rides feel pretty unappealing.

But if you’re considering taking up running as an off-season replacement, apply caution.

For beginners, the acute DOMS can be so devastating that a set of stairs can feel insurmountable. And more chronic conditions can crop up surprisingly fast. Tendinopathies will flare after even a fortnight of running beyond your experience.

The brutal demands of running are why any good training program will start with weeks of run-walk workouts.

These extra-easy “interval” sessions prepare the body for ground reaction forces more than three times a runner’s bodyweight. But be warned – they will do nothing for the fitness of even a moderately trained cyclist.

For noobs, the time investment is high, and the aerobic payoff is low.

Even veteran runners may feel little benefit when they return to the bike after spending winter pounding trails and tarmac – a recent study found no improvement in sport-specific performance if running and cycling were used to replace one another.

Because the mechanics simply don’t translate.

Even the most souplessed pedal stroke is a predominantly concentric (shortening/pushing) muscle contraction. Meanwhile, running incorporates an eccentric load into a push-pull motion that’s totally alien to even the strongest riders.

Running builds fitness, but it can only be expressed on the bike if you maintain the riding legs.

Riders who want to take up running to avoid the misery of the winter need to consider their longer-term goals.

If you’re in a rush to maintain bike fitness ahead of early-season challenges, look beyond the latest pair of Hokas.

The early run-walk protocols will wipe time off your schedule and do almost nothing for your aerobic capacity.

However, those who gamble by skipping those slightly embarrassing intervals are running toward injury.

Jayco-AlUla team trainer Peter Leo said the inefficiency of “learning” to run should give riders pause.…

"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.

"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.

"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.

He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".

"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.

A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.

In April, Google said people are now translating , external one trillion words a month with Google Translate.

That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatCGT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.

Direct sales of machine translation , external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.

"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.

Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.

"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.

But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.

"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman.

Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.

She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.

"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.

The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié.

When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".

In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.

The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.

Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.

"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.

She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).

"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.

She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon.

Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.

Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".

Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.

Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.

"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says François Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.…

Major tech firms have seen their stock values fall after a sell-off by investors following the US midterm elections.

The fall in the value of their shares across the world has been blamed on an expectation of a slowdown in AI development, although it comes after sharp rises over recent years.

As companies grow, they may issue shares. Many of the largest companies in the UK have shares which are bought and sold on the London Stock Exchange.

Their collective performance is often quoted amid a blizzard of numbers that may feel confusing and irrelevant.

Booms or falls in the stock market make the news, but rarely does anyone mention the FTSE 100 during a coffee with friends.

Yet, there are good reasons why this performance affects your life and finances.

Many people's initial reaction to "the markets" is that they are not directly affected, because they do not invest money.

Yet there are millions of people with a pension - either private or through work - who will see their savings (in what is known as a defined contribution pension) invested by pension schemes. The value of their savings pot is influenced by the performance of these investments.

Pension savers mostly let experts choose where to invest this money to help it grow. Widespread falls in share prices are likely to be bad news for pension savers.

Hundreds of billions of pounds are held in defined contribution pensions at the moment.

So big rises or falls can affect your pension, but the advice is to remember that pension savings, like any investments, are usually a long-term bet.

Experts say that investors have always had to ride economic shocks. Investments, by definition, require a long-term outlook and strategy. So, they are urging people not to panic in such circumstances or make knee-jerk decisions.

Some people have a pension which promises a specific value, depending on their salary. Others have no pension at all.

Millions of people have been automatically enrolled into a pension and may have not really noticed. Those schemes see employers divert wages into a pension and contribute some money themselves. The government adds a little in tax relief.

In every case, the value of these pension savings is affected by investment performance. So "the markets" matter - maybe not as much as everyday wages, but for future pensions.

Timing is more critical for those at retirement age, as this may be when a retiree uses their pension pot to buy a retirement income, or annuity. The bigger the pot, the more income they will get in retirement.

As you approach retirement age, pension pots tend to be moved to less risky investments, such as government bonds. When stock markets fall, these bonds can do better.

Anyone who has a pension pot invested and is taking an income from it will again see their investment go up and down with the stock markets.

That could mean getting less than you expected if you cash in too much after stock markets have fallen, making it important to plan how to make up any of this shortfall, experts say.

However, higher interest rates tend to mean better rates offered on annuities, and there is a chance of more rate rises in the UK by the Bank of England.

If share prices fall for an extended period then that could have an effect on jobs.

That's because investors in the company expect a return on that investment.

When it falls for a while, then they would expect the business to address issues, for example by cutting costs, and therefore jobs.

There is a huge element of the unknown here though. Companies have to consider lots of factors when making decisions on investment and employment.

In purely investment terms, lower share prices can offer an opportunity to buy, in the hope that over the long term, they recover and rise. Many people will do this initially through a stocks and shares Individual Savings Account (Isa).

However, it is worth noting that the sell-off in tech stocks in particular came after big rises, so long-term investors are still likely to have seen gains.

Experts and regulators are at pains to point out that investments can go down as well as up, and urge people not to put everything into one investment, but to diversify.

Some people invest money in what are known as tracker funds. These go up and down in line with the performance of a certain index, such as the FTSE 100.

So if the index falls, so does the value of their investments and vice versa. One advantage of these funds is that they often cost relatively little to sign up to.

Yes, and millions of people do, but experts stress that a long-term strategy is required to ride out short-term falls. It is also important to ensure cash savings are held too, so unexpected expenses - like the need for a replacement boiler - can be covered.

The government is keen to get people in the UK to invest more, partly because it says that will help UK economic growth and partly because it is much more popular among individuals in the US and some parts of Europe.

It backed an advertising campaign to encourage people to invest, funded by some of the UK's biggest financial services firms.

But the choice of "Savvy the Squirrel" to front the campaign has raised some eyebrows. Some question whether the push could get anywhere close to the success of the Tell Sid adverts of the 1980s, which encouraged people to invest in the newly privatised British Gas.

When we see big shifts in the stock markets there can also be fluctuations in the value of currencies and exchange rates.

As a result, prices could go up, but could also go down.

Upheaval to economies across the world, to oil prices and so on, have a big impact on what we pay at home for goods and services, so there are lots of factors in play.

Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have been climbing following an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.

Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.

However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.

On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.

But the Nasdaq Composite opened up on Friday and flattened out around 1.7% higher by lunchtime, reversing some of its 5.5% fall.

The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, was around 0.9% higher by lunchtime. The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened a little down before nudging into positive territory.

Nvidia, which shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, began Friday up more than 6% but settled around 4% higher as trading continued.

SpaceX and Tesla shares, which were also hammered on Thursday, saw more mixed gains, up more than 6% and nearly 5% respectively.

Chipmakers AMD and Micron both dropped by more than 17% on Thursday, but AMD shares had risen by about 12% on Friday while Micron was up more than 8%.

However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse on Friday.

The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.

In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.

In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.

"While no-one knows what happens next, it's clear that we've just seen a significant shift in market sentiment," he said.

"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?

Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck

The market fluctuations come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.

A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.

US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".

However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.

Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.

"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.

"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."

He said people were watching firms come into their communities and build data centres while their own energy costs were going up, and those companies "have to be better neighbours".

As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.

And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.

Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.

Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.

"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois.

The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma.

The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found.

For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator.

The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US.

Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases.

The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer.

They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms.

Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual.

Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the killer's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member.

"That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime.

It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year.

Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this."

The technique that led detectives to Zigler is credited with revolutionising how forensic cases are solved.

It has been highly successful in helping solve cases involving unidentified human remains and identifying suspects in longstanding investigations.

Othram claims it has helped solve thousands of cases. The company's chief executive David Mittelman likens investigative genetic genealogy to a GPS system: "The DNA profile is the GPS signal and it says 'you belong here.' But to understand where 'here' is, you need a map."

Public records, obituaries, and census data build that map so Othram's scientists can establish how different family trees connect.

However, Mittelman is quick to point out that DNA technology can only go so far before "a cascade of investigative steps" are needed.

DNA science isn't the only technology that are helping detectives solve cold cases.

One of the challenges facing detectives on major cases investigations like the hunt for Sperino's killer is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up.

Officers investigating Sperino's murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993.

They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case.

The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot.

This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence.

But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them."

Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique."

"But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds.

While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data.

"There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London. While one person may have opted in to their DNA being used, genetic relatives may not have given consent.

A lack of funding is another hurdle. Mittelman says: "Every law enforcement agency wants to do it. There's just not a lot of funding for it."

Sometimes cases are funded through donations or crowdfunding. Othram operates a website listing cases that members of the public can help fund.

While investigative genetic genealogy has been adopted in countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Australia, it is not yet used in the UK. The Home Office is conducting a study to consider whether it should be adopted in the UK but did not respond to a request for comment.

The UK is already in a strong position, says Syndercombe Court. "We have such an efficient DNA database that if you can get any DNA out of a crime scene, you've got over a 65% chance of putting a name to that person, which is enormously powerful," she says.

Rio Tinto is ploughing millions of dollars into stopping the poisonous cane toad reaching the Pilbara region of western Australia, where the mining giant has a vast iron ore operation.

The firm, alongside Curtin University in Perth and others, will spend A$28m (£14.5m) building a "toad containment zone" to prevent the pest travelling south.

While the cane toad is not a direct threat to Rio Tinto's business, it produces toxins lethal to native wildlife and poses a threat to Pilbara's ecosystem.

Rio Tinto has previously faced criticism for destroying two sacred Aboriginal rock shelters in Pilbara which sat above tonnes of iron ore.

The decision cost the former chief executive his job, provoked a widespread backlash and saw Rio Tinto commit to rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities.

Commenting on the proposed containment zone, Roberta Hunter, a ranger in Australia's Nyangumarta Warrarn Indigenous Protected Area, said: "Cane toads destroy the water and animals.

"When toads come close to our country, we want to be there to stop them because we don't want the country to be destroyed."

The plan is to cut off the toad's water supply by building a barrier across 7,500 sq km (2,895 sq m) of land between the Great Sandy Desert and the Indian Ocean.

In drier months, the cane toad needs water every few days to survive.

If there are no natural water sources, the toad relies on artificial water points normally used for cattle and irrigation.

The funding will be used to stop the toad accessing dams, storage tanks or other ground-level water sources. The five-year project will begin in 2027.

A number of native species are at risk if the toad gets into Pilbara. These include the northern quoll, whose numbers have been decreasing, the goanna lizard and the ghost bat.

The toads were introduced into Australia in 1935 to control beetles within the sugar cane industry.

Since then, they have been on a slow march west across the country's northern landscape, according to the Australian government, travelling between 40 km and 60 km a year.

There are no predators or diseases that control the toads, which defend themselves using poison.

Ben Phillips, a professor at Curtin University, said the toads would reach Pilbara within two decades without action.

He said: "The toad containment zone is a once in a lifetime opportunity to stop one of the world's worst invasive species in its tracks and protect the region's unique wildlife."

Tiara Allen arrived on time to interview for a retail job. Her interviewer didn't.

She waited for around 40 minutes in a shopping centre while the interviewer's co-worker called them "two or three times".

When they finally showed up, Tiara says she was told it was because the meeting wasn't in the schedule.

She needed work at the time, so took the job when she was offered it, but says she would handle the situation differently now.

"I would not take a job if they took that long," she says, adding that she believed her treatment during the interview was a sign of how the firm tended to treat staff.

Tiara is far from alone. She is one of many people who spoke to the BBC about their worst job interview experiences after we wrote about the one interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable .

While those situations can be hard to deal with in the moment, they can also teach us a lot about the world of work.

During an interview for an assistant at a book publisher in New York, Chas Edwards was asked a question he wasn't expecting.

"I was asked for my first job if I was a crier," he recalls.

Thinking the interviewer was being funny, Chas replied that he didn't cry. He was later told that this was why he got the job.

"Her last assistant had cried – too often, I guess? – and she wanted someone who didn't cry. So she was being serious and I thought it was a joke," he says.

It was a bad sign. Chas says it was "a terrible, terrible job with a miserable boss" and while he managed to make it through 13 months there without crying he was "crying inside".

"I set the world record for working for this person. No-one had ever lasted three months with her before," he recalls.

Despite all this, Chas says he is in some ways grateful the experience was so awful.

"Because every job since then, even the bad ones, are not that bad," he says, adding that he can "cry anywhere now".

Corinne Card also found herself floored when the first question she was asked in an interview for an administrative job was if she liked working with people.

When she replied yes, she was told that the job wouldn't be for her and the interview ended there.

"I don't know if it was a deliberate trap. Because who would answer 'I don't like working with people'?"

Corinne Mills, joint managing director of Personal Career Management, says that it can be worth asking an interviewer to clarify any weird questions, perhaps by repeating the question back to them.

However, if a line of questioning is really off-putting, she says it can also be a sign of what it's like to work there, saying that interviews are also about candidates judging the company.

Meanwhile, other questions are not just annoying – they are illegal.

Discrimination against a protected characteristic is against the law , external , meaning an employer cannot treat you less favourably based on your age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation.

Employment lawyer Roy Magara says that women being asked if they intend on having children in an interview is a "quite common" kind of bias. He says he has also seen a case where an older candidate was told he didn't get the job after an interview because he didn't fit the "vibe" of a younger team.

If you think these sorts of biases took place in your interview, Roy says you can send the company a subject access request , external to see how they discussed your application internally.

Worst-case scenarios like these can make interviews feel very difficult, especially considering the control employers have over candidates.

Euan Cameron, co-founder of hiring software Willo, says that even with this power imbalance it's important not to overthink what an interview is.

"An interview is just a conversation between two people," he says.

Of course, as in Tiara's case, it helps when both of those people show up.

On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China".

Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external

Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external

With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.

As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.

Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.

In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.

The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.

Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America

Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.

Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."

Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.

So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.

On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.

Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.

Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.

He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."

And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.

Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report , external at the start of this year.

Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.

The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.

Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.

From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.

Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.

Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.

Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.

Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.

This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.

This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.

"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.

The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.

That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.

"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.

If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.

While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.…

On Thursday, the Bank of England increased interest rates for the first time in over three years as it tries to get a grip on rising inflation linked to the Iran war.

Experts say there could be more hikes over the next 18 months, as the conflict continues to push up food, fuel and energy prices across the UK and worldwide.

Higher interest rates affect borrowing costs, however, which means mortgages, credit cards and personal loans could get more expensive for millions, even as savings rates improve.

For some, it could mean extra financial pressure at a time when they are already struggling with the cost of living. The BBC spoke to three people about how they could be affected.

Peter Gill, 48, is one of the around 1.3 million Britons on a variable rate mortgage.

These loans track the Bank of England base rate, with a margin on top determined by the lender, so any rise in interest rates can push up repayments.

Peter, who runs a small tiling business in Halifax, says his monthly repayments will go up by roughly £45 following Thursday's quarter-percentage point increase and he's worried they could climb higher.

But he still thinks it'd be more expensive to move onto a fixed-rate deal - which is when you pay a set amount of monthly interest for a period - and is prepared to stay put for now.

His higher mortgage costs come as the "cost of everything is going up", he says.

The father of two, who has a combined household income of £45,000 with his wife Faye, is having to pay his staff more because of increases in the national minimum wage. Raw material costs have also risen due to the war in Iran.

At home, the family's food, gas and electricity bills have gone up and he says he's working "about six and a half days a week" to shield them from the worst of it.

"From my point of view, inflation goes up which costs you, then interest rates go up and you have even less money."

Most UK mortgage holders are on fixed-rate deals, but that doesn't necessarily protect them when the Bank of England puts up rates.

David Hollingworth, from brokers L&C Mortgages, says many people will be shocked at how much higher fixed-rate deals are than they were five years ago following recent increases .

"Fixed rates have already risen due to market anticipation that interest rates would need to rise to combat higher inflation," he says.

Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living.

She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother of two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month.

"I don't know where that money is going to come from, it's something we are going to have to figure out as a family. It's stressful."

She and her husband, who have a joint income of about £70,000, have already gone through their direct debits and there's "no more obvious fat to trim".

There is also no scope for them to take on additional work, as they both work full time.

"We're still living in the same property, our household costs are remaining the same," Dawn says. "It's an additional cost of several hundred pounds but we're not getting anything extra for that."

When the Bank of England increases its base rate, credit card borrowing costs also tend to increase, although the impact is not always immediate.

It may affect people with outstanding debts, as providers can increase the interest rates they charge with 30 days' notice.

Ben Thomas, 41, from Shropshire, ditched his career as a chartered accountant during the Covid pandemic after a mental health crisis and retrained as a paramedic.

But the drop in income left him reliant on credit cards and personal loans for everyday living expenses and he is now £52,000 in debt.

Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?

Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you

Ben says he's reached an agreement to pause the interest on most of it, but he is still incurring charges on around £2,000 of credit card debt and is worried about his repayments going up.

"With all that's going on, rising interest rates is another cost to deal with," he tells the BBC.

As well as overall debt repayments of around £300 a month, he and his wife pay £760 on their mortgage. They have also struggled with higher food and energy bills.

Simon Trevethick is head of communications at StepChange, which has been helping Ben manage his debt. He says the debt charity has seen a 20% increase in people asking for support this year and warned of tougher times ahead.

"If higher borrowing costs feed through into household budgets over the coming months, we could see further pressure on people seeking support."

A second buyer has made a rescue bid for Poundland as the discount retailer teeters on the brink of collapse, with thousands of jobs at risk.

London-based Xyra Group has offered to pay off half of Poundland's outstanding debts - a key sticking point in takeover talks so far - immediately. The rest would be deferred.

With Poundland close to collapse, US-based owners Gordon Brothers have already rejected a rival bid from an Irish property group which would have saved its 12,000 staff.

Gordon Brothers said the business has faced years of instability and "remains challenged and vulnerable".

Sources familiar with the offer said Xyra is offering to immediately pay off £12.5m of an outstanding £30m loan on Poundland's books.

The offer came as Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds held crunch talks with Gordon Brothers about the future of the business, urging the investment firm to protect staff however possible.

Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for £1 last June, committed at the meeting to prioritise offers which protect its shops and workers.

The company said: "We are pursuing all avenues through the sale process to find a solution which protects as many jobs as possible and preserves value. Work continues at pace, engaging in active discussions on offers with interested parties."

Xyra is offering to pay off a higher proportion of Poundland's outstanding debts than Martin Property Group, which previously submitted a bid that Gordon Brothers rejected.

But doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer, as there is little evidence they meet Gordon Brothers' tests, including whether they have the money and whether they would be good long-term owners of Poundland.

Sources pointed to the appointment of Andrew Brode to Xyra's board as a sign of its credibility. Brode works for RWS - a company that provides AI solutions for businesses.

Judith MacKenzie, head of Downing Fund Managers, told the BBC Brode is "well known and very credible" among small businesses in the UK.

But she said there is "hardly any information" publicly available about Xyra. "So, although some of the people look good, I can't find any evidence to say that they've got the money to back it up yet," MacKenzie added.

Gordon Brothers said: "Our intent throughout the comprehensive sale process has been to protect as many jobs as possible and preserve value in order to deliver the best available outcome for all the people, creditors and local communities who care about this business as much as we do."

Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of Poundland has not yet been made.

Though Xyra made an offer to take over the whole business, it is unclear whether it would keep Poundland together as its owner or break the company up.

Several Poundland suppliers have said they would also go bust if the retailer collapses. Its founder Steve Smith said two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, those who solely work for Poundland, would be caught up in the collapse.

He added that not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall.

Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm

Poundland owner in crunch talks as retailer's collapse looms

The pound has risen to its highest overall level since the Brexit referendum over a decade ago.

Sterling has risen notably in recent weeks against the euro and the dollar, ahead of an expected rise in interest rates.

The most-watched measure of the value of the British currency against a basket of 18 of the world's main currencies this week reached its joint highest level since the June 2016 referendum, according to Bank of England figures.

The value reached 86.4 on an index where 100 equals the value in 2005. The Bank will officially confirm the calculation on Thursday.

The value of sterling fell significantly after the Brexit referendum in June 2016, and reached further lows during the Brexit process, the Covid pandemic and the 2022 mini-Budget.

Some traders said the UK was being seen in a different light given relative political stability, solid growth and the rapprochement with the European Union.

Sterling has responded strongly to Brexit developments and political uncertainty in recent years.

Jim O'Neill, an economist and former Treasury minister, said: "I'm not surprised. People were, and to a lesser extent, are, underestimating the improving momentum in the UK,"

A stronger pound can help rein in inflation, and increase buying power for consumers on imports and on holidays.

UK growth so far this year has outperformed all forecasts, but there are signs that higher energy and fuel prices have now hit consumer confidence.

The Bank's nine member Monetary Policy Committee faces an important decision on interest rates on Thursday, with the first rise in three years widely expected.

On Wednesday sterling was up 0.28% against the dollar at $1.3434 and was flat against the euro at €1.1996 as of 23:01 GMT.

Before joining Morrisons, Potts was chief executive of Tesco's Irish business, its UK arm and its Asian operation.

According to Asda, Leighton had planned to step aside from the day-to-day running of the group, after he returned in 2024, more than two decades after serving as chief executive.

"Over the last two years, we have stabilised the business and returned it to some growth," said Leighton.

"David has an outstanding record in our industry, his experience is exactly what we now require for the next stage of our transformation and beyond and it will be great to work with him."

Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.

Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing.

She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation.

A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media.

Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others.

"A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood.

AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts , but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's.

Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement.

Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI.

"My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel.

Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company.

CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI.

"We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell.

"We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way."

Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role."

If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier.

Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires.

For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer , external , it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building.

Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%.

Cian Clinton, who joined consultancy Valliance last September after graduating from a Bachelor of Science in 2024, says the incorporation of AI into his role makes him feel less like a graduate, and more like an equal team member. He uses around 10 AI agents daily for different tasks.

"Your ideas and your creativity are a lot more valued because you actually get to implement those firsthand, and the responsibility you take on is a lot greater because of that," says London-based Clinton, 23.

"I am now taking on responsibilities which would usually take me four or five years to get to."

His career progression, he believes, will now be faster as a result.

"AI is killing the 'pyramid' approach…progression is no longer based on your knowledge bank. Now it's more based on your critical thinking and understanding of the processes," says Clinton.

There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers.

But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?

Underwood says she'd like to still pick up the traditional PR skills her role isn't currently focused on, but is confident of her future in the agency's growing AI team.

"There's certain things that I haven't had the chance to do yet, like directly pitching to the media. I absolutely plan to do this," she says.

Graduates becoming too AI-centric is an issue for Simon Pratt, chief operating officer at Portman Finance Group. He says being able to use AI effectively is important, but the company's two-year graduate programme is fully centred on "learning the trade".

"Our graduates rotate across four areas at six-month intervals, working directly alongside senior relationship managers to learn their trade," Northampton-based Pratt explains.

"They'll learn all of our financial products, how to draft credit papers for submission to lenders, and how to build meaningful relationships with our customers. They'll progress to running transactions from start to finish."

Claire Reed, PwC UK's chief technology and innovation officer, believes graduate roles that are too AI heavy won't necessarily provide graduates long-term career progression.

"There will be no graduate job now that doesn't require a baseline of AI literacy," says Glasgow-based Reed.…
