One look at the Premier League table shows why Carrick is right not to get carried away.

If results go against them, Manchester United could be bottom of the table by the time they kick-off against Aston Villa on Sunday.

Neither Mourinho nor Solskjaer could follow up their 3-2 successes with another victory. Mourinho's United drew at Chelsea, then lost at home to Juventus. Solskjaer's United were embarrassed by Liverpool. It meant neither man was able to build on the momentum generated by their epic victories.

United have gone seven Premier League games without a win. They went eight under Ruben Amorim at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, but draws and losses were split by victories en route to the Europa League final, so the effect was not as great as it feels right now.

The club does have an exceptional home record against Villa. They have won their past six in all competitions and lost just two league games against the Midlands outfit at Old Trafford since 1983.

When United sources finally communicated - almost 48 hours after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October - that Carrick and his players would be given the opportunity to turn the situation around, no timescale was put on this. However, the feeling was the forthcoming international break would be an appropriate time for the club hierarchy to take stock and decide what direction they should go in.

In the two games since, Carrick's team have been excellent across two halves.

Victory against Villa, albeit with £70m Carlos Baleba joining the injured list, would haul them up to within two points of Unai Emery's side heading into a tricky run of matches post international break, starting at Liverpool, but also including trips to Newcastle and Arsenal in December. Given he beat Manchester City and Arsenal in his first two games as interim boss.

Defeat is likely to dump them in the relegation zone for at least a fortnight and facing severe baiting at Anfield on 22 November.

"It's not about me," is a phrase Carrick has repeated often as he has assessed the wreckage of another bad result. The outcome against Roma was much more positive.

There is no suggestion Carrick's future has been decided just yet. What happens at Old Trafford this weekend looks very important.

When Sir Jim Ratcliffe became a co-owner of Manchester United in 2024, much of the narrative centred on his desire to rebuild the club around a British core.

Given the expense of buying homegrown players, and the difficulties Michael Carrick - the first permanent British managerial appointment of the Ineos era - has faced this season, perhaps Ratcliffe is rethinking.

But if Carrick fails to stop the rot and loses his job, United are already considering the merits of appointing another British coach - albeit one who is more experienced.

That Eddie Howe is a contender for a job that remains one of the most high-profile in world football isn't hard to fathom.

Speak to those who have worked alongside Howe and they describe a man whose track record of improving players is a direct result of his relentless approach on the training field.

They will also tell you Howe is someone who places an unwavering importance on the methodology of setting a winning culture.

Howe may lack experience at one of the traditional top-six clubs, but his body of work at Bournemouth and Newcastle is impressive.

Of course, managing Manchester United is an altogether different proposition.

Indeed, Howe's emergence as a potential successor to Carrick has been greeted with negativity in some circles.

Sections of the fanbase have been vocal on social media with their opinion that Howe isn't a big enough name to replace Carrick.

Former United players Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt also fell short of providing their backing to Howe on their podcast, though it is worth pointing out they spoke in favour of the 48-year-old's potential appointment when Ruben Amorim was sacked in January.

Ex-captain Roy Keane is among those to have backed Howe as a possible successor to Carrick, and other former top-flight players - including Darren Bent, Gareth Barry and Jack Wilshere - have also touted him as the man for the job.

Of course, if you look hard enough you'll find voices for and against every potential manager, and it will be up to United chief executive Omar Berrada, sporting director Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell to weigh up how they proceed.

Their first decision will be what happens with Carrick, and Saturday's match against Chelsea is likely to have a bearing on how United move forward.

If Carrick does depart, finances will inevitably be a factor.

The former Middlesbrough boss and his staff will need to be paid up before United even get to factoring in the monetary commitment towards their next head coach.

While the details of Howe's agreement with Newcastle when he left in the summer remain confidential, it is understood that as things stand any club or national team would be required to pay a seven-figure compensation fee to the Magpies.

Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that Newcastle - with a view to protecting themselves against Howe walking straight into another club - reached an agreement over a compensation structure that decreases over time.

It is understood that figure started at £6m but has already reduced by half.

The compensation payments have an expiry date - understood to be before the end of the season - at which point he can be appointed for nothing.

Of course, in an industry in which astronomical figures are the norm, the prospect of paying a maximum of £3m for Howe may not be too problematic.

That said, given the amount Manchester United have spent on hiring and firing managers in recent years, it is understandable if Berrada and Wilcox want to keep costs down.

How talking about Man Utd's cycle of doom became an industry

As well as the doubts from some supporters about Howe's potential appointment, there has also been conjecture over how he would fit in United's footballing structure.

At both Bournemouth and Newcastle, Howe developed a strong powerbase in all aspects of the footballing department - including recruitment.

That dynamic wasn't without financial benefit to Howe's employers.

The likes of Nathan Ake, Callum Wilson and Tyrone Mings were all signed by Howe at Bournemouth - and sold for a big profit by the Cherries.

At Newcastle, meanwhile, Howe was instrumental in the signings of Bruno Guimarares, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Alexander Isak - all of whom were sold for more than they joined for. Dan Burn, Lewis Hall and Tino Livramento are among those to have developed into full England internationals under his coaching.

But with a football management structure at Old Trafford that includes Berrada, Wilcox and Vivell, it is likely that Howe - at least not immediately - would not be afforded the same level of autonomy.

Howe, though, is on record saying he is happy to work alongside sporting directors, and has a track record of doing so - firstly at Bournemouth under Richard Hughes, then chief executive Neill Blake.

At Newcastle, he worked closely with senior management figures Dan Ashworth, Amanda Staveley and Mehrdad Ghodoussi - so fitting into Manchester United's structure wouldn't be drastically different.

Whether he would want the job given the challenges, we may never know. And ultimately it is the opinion of Manchester United's decision-makers that will truly matter.

Howe is an obvious contender for the Manchester United job, just as he would be if the England head coach's position became available.

Whether he is offered it or not will give a clear indication about the path United are going down.…

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.

The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.

It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"

Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.

"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.

"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.

"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.

"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"

And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.

This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".

"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.

It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.

"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.

Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.

"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.

"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"

Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.

"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.

In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.

He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.

"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."

Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.

The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.

Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.

But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.

By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.

It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.

"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."

Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.

Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.

"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.

At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.

This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.

By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.

So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.

Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.

Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".…

He's been around the block a few times. His career has not been especially stellar. He has a reputation for falling out with teams and team-mates. And there is a new generation breaking through in F1, led by new world champion Kimi Antonelli.

The catalyst for Ocon's departure from Haas was a falling-out with team principal Ayao Komatsu after Friday practice in Mexico City last weekend.

Exactly what led to him being dropped is unknown. No-one is talking, not even off the record, and lawyers are now involved.

What is known is that Ocon objected over the team radio while in the car to being told by his engineer Laura Mueller that they were switching his run plan from using soft tyres for his race-simulation run to mediums.

That followed a report in France's L'Equipe newspaper saying a meeting between Komatsu and Ocon "ended abruptly, perhaps even physically".

Haas said nothing more over the weekend in Mexico but on Tuesday evening put out what was already being seen as the inevitable announcement that he would not drive for the team again.

Haas had already run out of patience with Ocon long before Mexico City but whatever happened there was serious enough that Komatsu felt the relationship had to end on the spot.

The decline of Ocon's time with Haas has echoes of previous experiences.

Ocon has been beaten by team-mate Oliver Bearman over his two seasons at Haas, just as he was outpaced by Pierre Gasly and before him Fernando Alonso at Alpine, and Daniel Ricciardo before that when the team was known as Renault.

When Haas signed Ocon, his reputation was such that many were surprised they had taken him. Komatsu felt he could make it work.

But the team began to notice a pattern. When Ocon was struggling, he would become defensive and blame the team and car. Tensions would rise and the team felt there was a lack of accountability from the driver.

There were also clashes with his team-mate, for example in Monaco practice when they got in each other's way and Bearman ended up calling Ocon "an idiot" over the radio.

They also crashed into each other towards the end of the British Grand Prix last year.

Competitive tensions between team-mates are common in F1. A driver's team-mate is also their biggest rival - the only person with the same equipment so the only driver against which they can be directly measured.

The parallel need to work together to benefit the team's overall prospects can be an uncomfortable ask in such circumstances.

It's a problem that is causing tension at Ferrari between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, for example, as was also seen in Mexico.

But over the years, Ocon has built an unenviable reputation for both these sides of his character. To outsiders, this can be surprising because he is charm personified with the media, a delight to deal with.

He and Gasly - who were childhood friends before falling out nearly 20 years ago - crashed twice together at Alpine. The end of their two seasons together was the first occasion on which Ocon was released before the end of the season, dropped with one race to go.

Alonso and Ocon also fell out and the Spanish icon did not trouble to hide his distaste for his team-mate's behaviour at times. Ocon also had on-track clashes and team radio disputes with Sergio Perez when at Force India.

Alpine also saw the same pattern as did Haas more recently in terms of self-awareness and accountability.

Alonso put in a starring performance in wet qualifying in Canada in 2022 and stuck his midfield Alpine on the front row alongside Max Verstappen's Red Bull.

That lap was 1.6 seconds faster than Ocon's and team insiders say he simply could not accept that he had been that much slower.

All drivers complain. It's part of their make-up. Their motivation comes from believing they can be the best, and finding weaknesses in the car and improving them is their job and how they make themselves and the team more competitive.…

When the McLaren pit crew refuelled a car, changed its tyres and relayed information to their driver in less than seven seconds at the Spanish Grand Prix in 2001, they were just doing their jobs.

But 700 miles away in the break room at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), Dr Martin Elliott and his colleagues were watching after completing a life-saving operation on a young child.

The brief glimpse would change how the doctors approached patient care. From surgery-to-ICU handovers and neonatal care to air-ambulance response times, F1's innovations have made an impact far beyond the track.

At Ferrari's factory in Maranello, the medical team studied how pit crews organised roles, communication and handovers.

Doctors and nurses started each procedure with a checklist, setting out specific roles and tasks. This reduced human error and helped ensure key tasks were completed. All patient data was also shared from the operating theatre to the care unit.

Gaps in performance were identified and addressed, while repeated rehearsals helped refine the process.

As a result, the process from surgery to intensive care became more organised, and a 2007 study by researchers at GOSH and the University of Oxford found the F1-inspired handover process reduced technical errors, information omissions and handover time.

Reflecting on the project, Dr Elliott, then a consultant paediatric cardiothoracic surgeon at GOSH, said: "The environment we were working in then and in many ways still do is fundamentally potentially dangerous at every step.

"And of course, fundamentally, that's how F1 doesn't make mistakes. They have created an environment of complete precision, not only in engineering, but also in process, because they simply can't afford financially or from a race perspective to slip up.

"It's the same, you know, the precious parcel on the trolley is the same as the precious parcel in the car. You have to get all of those steps right."

The model was later adopted by other healthcare teams.

Fifteen years ago, Williams worked with the University Hospital of Wales to improve neonatal resuscitation.

Former Williams human performance specialist Gemma Fisher recognised that the organisation of pit-crew equipment to prevent delay could also be applied in a hospital setting.

Video analysis unveiled the chaotic reality of medical emergencies with overlapping voices and misplaced equipment.

Standardising roles - deciding who stood where, who needed to be heard at what moment and where equipment was stationed - allowed for a faster, more efficient response.

Debriefings allowed medical staff to review what had happened and identify what could be improved for future emergencies.

The changes also encouraged junior doctors to raise concerns without fear of blame.

The collaboration extended beyond working practices and into engineering. Advanced Healthcare Technology and Williams have since developed the Babypod: a carbon fibre carrier designed to withstand a 20G crash, which can help prevent injury in the transportation of babies from ambulance to hospital.

F1 continues to find new ways to apply its expertise in emergency medicine.

At this year's race at Silverstone, a collaboration with Air Ambulance Cornwall showed how response times could be improved, with take-off time reduced from five minutes to three and a half.

This was achieved using many of the same methods, including quick and organised starts, having equipment ready for use and clear communication across the team.

David Richards, chairman of Motorsport UK and former team principal of BAR and Benetton, said: "You might not see one and a half minutes in the overall scheme of things, but one and a half minutes when you're lying by the side of the road or you've fallen off a horse or you've fallen down a cliff and you've hurt yourself, those minutes must seem like years for the person who's injured."

Richards said the partnership would continue to look for ways to reduce response times further.

Twenty-five years after Dr Elliott first saw a pit stop that inspired a new way of thinking, lessons from the sport continue to influence healthcare, from neonatal treatment to emergency response.

Wolff's claim about this being Antonelli's best performance so far might surprise anyone who watched him win his home grand prix at Monza from 19th on the grid.

When this was pointed out, Wolff replied: "My problem is that I don't remember past races. So now you're saying Monza was actually also pretty good, obviously with the advantage of the home crowd and seeing all these tifosi that were a little bit confused, wearing red, and an Italian with the Mercedes outfit up on the podium. And I think we're going to see more Kimi caps, Mercedes caps next year.

"So both of them were pretty good. But the headline that this is the best we can keep."

Antonelli agreed. "Monza, we clearly had the fastest car," he said. "We were just super quick, so of course it was incredibly special coming from the back. But it was also a track where it was relatively easy to overtake, and we were so quick.

"Definitely, Monza was a super-special one, and one that I will remember forever. But this one probably, in terms of execution, was better, because the way we built up and the way we built the performance throughout the weekend was very good."

Mercedes went to Austin with both cars in the new upgraded specification that had proved unconvincing, to say the least, when it made its debut in Malaysia two races ago.

There, Wolff said he thought it had made the car 0.3secs per lap slower. The team split the cars in Singapore to try to understand the package better, and then used it on both cars in Austin. Antonelli stuck it on pole and dominated the race. Russell's performance looked more like the one the car produced in Malaysia.

"The update we put on the car is difficult to operate," Wolff said. "And Kimi landed it.

"Maybe it's a bit harsh to say but I think his driving style just glues with the car. We saw that in qualifying yesterday where on his last lap he could have been another 0.15-0.2 secs up. And on the other side George just struggled so much. And I believe this is because the operational window of the car is so difficult."

When Antonelli clinches the title, he will become the first Italian to do so since Alberto Ascari in 1953. It's a remarkable statistic for a country which is so engrained in the sport, and it certainly resonates with his compatriots.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "As an Italian, wow, we need to go back to Ascari, the names that they created the inspiration for all of us. To see an Italian achieving this level of performance and results in Formula 1, that's particularly thrilling, as an Italian person in motorsport."

Stella's answer continued into an area that begins to explain the way in which he has proved so superior to Russell this year.

"Going more into the technical, and specifically this season, Kimi is a very interesting one to look at, because he pretty much attacks all the times," Stella said.

"You see how often he's just going off track, and you see his onboard (camera), he's pretty aggressive. But at the same time, this seems to be not only kind of an aggressive driving, or an attacking driving, but effective.

"And if we think how much we talk in these media sessions about the cars being difficult to drive consistently fast, it should be recognised how much he's been able to harness his driving style with what is required of the cars.

"But at the same time, almost contradicting what I'm saying, when is the time to bring home the result, he's been able to do it.

"So he's the deserving leader of this championship. He's writing an important piece of history for motorsport, because once he achieves the championship, he will be the youngest."…

Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli became Formula 1's youngest world champion by finishing third at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the race, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton finishing second.

Hamilton was unhappy with his team-mate Charles Leclerc and said Ferrari "have to have some serious talks behind closed doors" after fighting between their two drivers cost them victory in Mexico.

BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

McLaren has its 'papaya' rules, is it now time for Ferrari to introduce its 'Maranello' rules? - John

The battle between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc on the opening lap in Mexico, and the fall-out from it, provided a perfect illustration of the problems that can arise when a team has two top drivers of equal status.

Hamilton's point after the race was that Ferrari would have won the race - probably got a one-two - if the pair had worked together on that first lap.

"When your team-mate works against you and then you lose positions like that, it's definitely tough," he said.

Team boss Frederic Vasseur aldo bemoaned the loss of a potential one-two, admitting he was "frustrated".

Leclerc argued that it takes two to tango. "I could be also unhappy with how much he pushed me off track out of Turn One," he said, "but it is racing. When you are fighting for a win it is the way it should be."

Leclerc added: "At the end we both did a mistake going into Turn Four. It's not like we had contact whatsoever. We both went straight and that gave the opportunity for Max to overtake. So I don't think it should be that much of a talking point."

Clearly there is a problem here. It's not the first time the Ferrari drivers' competing priorities have caused issues this year, and Vasseur has yet to find a way to manage it effectively, and get the drivers to buy into what he decides.

In this case, the two drivers are expressing two completely different, but valid, points of view.

Hamilton is thinking of the team result - which conveniently also meant a win for him - Leclerc primarily about the fact that they are allowed to race for the win.

The problem is that the team's result was compromised and a win thrown away.

Had Verstappen not passed Hamilton as a consequence of the incident, Leclerc could have given the place back by Turn 11 as was required by the rules.

But once Verstappen was between them, continuing in the lead was Leclerc's only realistic option.

This is a really difficult situation for Vasseur to handle.

The team wants to win the race as first priority, but the same applies to each individual driver. Sometimes those two competing priorities clash.

And if Ferrari ever get themselves a car that can compete for the title, it will only get harder, because the stakes for both drivers are then much higher.

McLaren have done better at handling this, and Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have been more acquiescent, but even their approach has led them into problems, as happened a number of times last year. And sometimes the drivers ignore it, as with the crash between the two drivers in the sprint in Singapore.

Vasseur's problem is that if he had asked the drivers not to race on the first lap on Sunday, he would have been essentially asking Leclerc to hand Hamilton a win. And how do you keep an ambitious driver happy in that situation?

One also has to ask whether, if the situations were reversed, Hamilton would accept the same request.

Hamilton revealed after the race that Ferrari "don't have rules of engagement, and whether or not that would change anything from Charles' side, I don't know".

McLaren have rules of engagement. One is not to crash into each other. That's not what happened here. Another is that the team result comes first. But it's very hard to come up with specific rules that would deal with a live racing situation such as this.

One could argue all day about the rights and wrongs and who could have done what to engineer a better outcome.

As Hamilton said: "We've just got to figure out. But something needs to change for sure."

Given that Yamaha have withdrawn from MotoGP in Qatar (and, I understand, much of the media aren't going), why is F1 still so intent on going? The US mid-terms are potentially a trigger point. The risk seems too high. - Richard

This weekend's Qatar MotoGP has been a subject of controversy in motorcycle racing in the context of the war in the Middle East.

First, the vast majority of riders wrote a letter to the sport's bosses saying they would prefer not to race there, and at the weekend Yamaha pulled out of the race, citing a company-wide travel policy.

The race is still going ahead. MotoGP, like F1, is owned by US group Liberty Media.

Similar concerns also exist within F1 on a widespread basis about the end-of-season races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi going ahead.

Privately, many people within the sport have significant misgivings about going to the Middle East, but those opinions are by and large not being voiced publicly.

One person who has done so is Williams driver Carlos Sainz, who said at the US Grand Prix: "(The sport's bosses) seem very convinced that it's going to go ahead.

"On my personal side, and not speaking as the GPDA, it's very difficult to be convinced right now because there are still things happening in the Middle East, and also there is obviously an election that is going to happen in the US and things that are going to happen on the political side of the world that could affect the next month, month and a half, very suddenly.

"So, I think it's relatively premature to be so convinced."

It's hard to argue with the factual basis for those remarks. Nevertheless, Sainz and Williams were subsequently spoken to by F1, after which Williams put out a statement "clarifying" his remarks.

F1's argument is that it has no reason to cancel the races.…

Another strong weekend that deserved more. Qualified seventh and had his race badly compromised when Russell spun him on lap one, so recovering to ninth after penalties were applied was decent.

Manuel Fantini's eyes are wide with excitement. There's a broad grin on his face.

Fantini is recalling the first time he saw Kimi Antonelli behind the wheel of a car - well, a go-kart.

"When I first saw him, I said: 'Mamma mia, chi diavolo è questo?' In English that means, 'Oh Mama, who the hell is this one?'"

"He was six years old. When you go to the track for the first time, it's normal you go too fast and take turns the wrong way.

"But he was improving with each lap, like he'd known the track for years. At the end of that day, he was faster than the others and with a kart slower than them. Absurd! Incredible!"

Fantini is speaking to BBC Sport in a small cafe in Forli, Bologna. The autumnal sun creates a glare as the light bounces off the sign of the adjacent racetrack - Galliano Park.

Owned by the Fantini family for almost 30 years, it's where Antonelli first climbed into a go-kart. It had to be adapted because he wasn't tall enough to reach the throttle or brake pedals.

"His priority was being better - not being faster," says Fantini. "That is the key in motorsport to be a champion.

"Everyone thinks you must be fast, but the approach of Kimi is the correct approach.

"He had something immediately in his veins that was not normal. If you're only fast, you can hurt yourself or make mistakes."

A former racer himself, Fantini says he is proud to have been a small part in Antonelli's journey to becoming Formula 1's youngest world champion.

He is sure the 20-year-old's achievement will lift the whole country - but even more so the people of Bologna, where Antonelli was born and still visits regularly.

"I am very proud of him," says Fantini. "And I'm very proud of his parents because the most difficult thing nowadays is when you have so much talent, to keep the kid safe and with humility.

"I see the same incredible person. He is so natural, so funny and good as a kid. But when he puts on the helmet… pay attention."

Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' who started driving on dad's lap

It has been 73 years since Italy had a Formula 1 drivers' champion. For a country synonymous with speed, it's been a torturous experience.

Perhaps the highlight of Antonelli's season was winning the Italian Grand Prix from 19th on the grid - showing the mastery and bravery many predict will mean he dominates the sport for years to come.

After victory at Monza, Antonelli was pictured eating pasta out of his winner's trophy. The dish - tagliatelle al ragu - was a nod to his Bolognese roots and a region famed for its cuisine.

About an hour from Forli is Bologna's city centre. Down a side street is Trattoria dal Biassanot - a restaurant in which Antonelli regularly dines.

You might think its walls would be littered with photos of his visits, but there is not a single one.

Owner Luca Bugamelli explains: "Kimi is just one of us. We've known Kimi since he was a child. He comes here with his father, mother and sister and there's a lot of moments we eat at the same table.

"This region loves motorsport. Kimi is the God of the land."

Antonelli's rapid rise has given Italians something of a dilemma, though.

Italy is famed for circuits including Imola and Monza, and is home to two of the world's most famous high-performance car manufacturers - Ferrari and Lamborghini.

When it comes to F1, it's almost sporting blasphemy for an Italian to cheer on anyone but Ferrari - but Antonelli drives for the German-owned Mercedes team.

"I had some friends that went to Monza - and probably for the first time in the history, the crowd is split for Ferrari and Kimi," says Paolo - a resident of Bologna we encounter proudly wearing a Ferrari-emblazoned jumper.

"Kimi walks around the city sometimes. He'll go to the stadium to watch Bologna Football Club. He's very integrated in the city. I saw him last month in a bar."

Antonelli 'disrupting rules of fandom' in Ferrari's Italy

As well as endearing himself to lifelong motorsport fans, Antonelli has also amassed a legion of non-aficionados thanks - in large part - to his social media presence.

The shops and billboards of Bologna are not yet littered with his image - but his achievement is far reaching.

"I feel very proud that a person from these streets could be so famous and win so many things," says Somaya - a 20-year-old student.

"It makes me feel proud to be from here. It's inspiring."

Italy is beaming with pride. All thanks to a boy from Bologna who became a man in Monza before sealing his F1 fairytale by clinching the world title in Mexico.

How much do you know about F1 champion Antonelli?

Kimi Antonelli has made history by becoming the youngest title winner in the 77th year of the Formula 1 World Championship.

The Italian, at 20 years and 68 days, has beaten the record of Sebastian Vettel, who was 23 years and 134 days old when he won the first of his four drivers' championships in 2010.

Antonelli, who was still a teenager until 25 August, has secured the title in his second season in the sport.

We take a look at F1's other young champions and how Antonelli's achievement compares with theirs.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Second full season

F1 debut: 2025 Australian Grand Prix (aged 18)

Antonelli has already broken a number of records on the way to becoming F1's youngest champion.

In his second season, he became the youngest driver to achieve a pole position in China and the youngest to lead the championship at the next race in Japan.

In Monaco, he became the youngest driver to complete a 'grand slam' of pole position, fastest lap, leading every lap and winning the race.

All this after a rookie season in 2025 in which there were occasional highs but plenty of errors, and his final total of 150 points was less than half of the 319 accumulated by Mercedes team-mate George Russell.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Third full season

Vettel was one of four drivers who could win the title going into the season-ending 2010 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

He was far from the best placed, though, trailing Ferrari's Fernando Alonso by 15 points before the race and his Red Bull team-mate Mark Webber by seven.

The German did what he had to do by winning the grand prix and Alonso could only finish seventh, having become stuck behind the Renault of Vitaly Petrov.

With Webber in eighth, Vettel won the championship by four points from Alonso.

It was yet another F1 record for Vettel. He had become the youngest F1 points scorer on his debut for BMW Sauber in Indianapolis in 2007, before becoming the then youngest pole sitter and race winner at the 2008 Italian Grand Prix for Toro Rosso.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Second full season

F1 debut: 2007 Australian Grand Prix (aged 22)

Lewis Hamilton's debut season in 2007 almost delivered a fairytale title but he faltered in the final two races of the year.

He failed to score in China and finished seventh in Brazil, which allowed Ferrari's Kimi Raikkonen to pip both Hamilton and fellow McLaren driver Fernando Alonso by a single point.

Somehow the climax to the 2008 championship, also in Brazil, was even more dramatic.

Hamilton was battling for the title with Ferrari's home favourite Felipe Massa and the Briton's fourth place was going to be enough to secure the crown when a late rain shower changed everything.

Leader Massa and Hamilton were among those who changed to intermediate tyres but Toyota's Timo Glock stayed out, which lifted him up to fourth.

Hamilton, now in fifth, had Toro Rosso's Vettel right behind him and couldn't afford to lose another position. With just over two laps to go, he ran wide and Vettel was through.

Massa crossed the line to win the race with Hamilton still sixth. The Ferrari pit crew, Massa's family and the Brazilian fans celebrated but with the rain intensifying, Glock was slowing on his dry-weather tyres and Hamilton passed him into the final corner to take the title by a single point. It was heart-stopping stuff.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Fourth full season

F1 debut: 2001 Australian Grand Prix (aged 19)

Alonso established control of the 2005 championship early in the season by winning four of the first seven races and never relinquished it.

The Spaniard's speed and consistency ensured he prevailed over Raikkonen, whose McLaren-Mercedes was fast but fragile. A third place at the Brazilian Grand Prix was enough to give Alonso the title with two races to spare.

He won a second consecutive title in 2006, also for Renault, and the 45-year-old remains one of the great personalities and outstanding talents in F1.

He'll be back for another season with Aston Martin in 2027, 26 years after his debut for Minardi.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Seventh full season

F1 debut: 2015 Australian Grand Prix (aged 17)

Hamilton won the title on the final lap of the 2008 season but he would lose it on the final lap in 2021 in circumstances that remain a source of huge controversy.

His rival in a thrilling and intense season-long duel was Red Bull's Max Verstappen. There were plenty of flashpoints along the way and it all came to a climax in Abu Dhabi.

Verstappen and Hamilton went into the final race of the season level on points. The Dutchman qualified on pole but Mercedes' Hamilton beat him off the line and largely controlled the race thereafter, until Williams' Nicholas Latifi crashed with five laps to go, bringing out a safety car.

Hamilton did not have enough of an advantage over second-placed Verstappen to pit for fresh tyres and maintain the lead, so stayed out. Verstappen, with nothing to lose, came in and fitted softs.

Race director Michael Masi allowed the lapped cars between Hamilton and Verstappen to go past, but not those behind the Red Bull. He allowed the race to restart for one final racing lap and Verstappen overtook Hamilton, who was a sitting duck on his old hard tyres.

Verstappen and Hamilton, in their own ways, were both stunned and Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff shouted over the radio to Masi: "No, Michael, no! That was so not right!"

As happened with Vettel from 2010-13, this was the first of four consecutive titles for a Red Bull driver with Verstappen dominating the 2022, 2023 and 2024 seasons.

Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Second full season

F1 debut: 1970 British Grand Prix (aged 23)

The drivers' title is sewn up, and the constructors' may well be on Sunday, but Formula 1 marches restlessly, relentlessly on.

This weekend's Sao Paulo Grand Prix is in many ways the first page of the first chapter of the next championship battle.

New world champion Kimi Antonelli says he sees the final races of the season as preparation to defend his title in 2027, and his vanquished Mercedes team-mate George Russell is working on understanding where things went wrong, with the aim of putting them right.

The team's main target this weekend is securing the three points more than Ferrari they need to lock away the constructors' championship, to underline their return to the form they showed for so long in the 2010s.

Mercedes' rivals, meanwhile, are continuing the work that has seen them turn what was a chasm in performance at the beginning of the year into a highly competitive battle between the top four teams at the end.

The season has been in two parts. Mercedes dominated the first third, winning seven of the first eight races.

Since then, Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull have all had their time in the sun, and out of the past 12 races, Mercedes have won six, Red Bull three, McLaren two and Ferrari one.

Only the beginnings of a competitive picture have emerged in Sao Paulo, with Antonelli and Lando Norris in an upgraded McLaren initially appearing in good shape in Friday practice, but beyond that there are a number of running narratives to maintain the interest.

Chief among them is the tension between Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc after they contrived to throw away a potential one-two finish in Mexico last Sunday by tangling on the first lap.

After that race, Hamilton said the team had "big problems" and needed "serious talks".

Those happened on Thursday evening, after Leclerc and team principal Frederic Vasseur arrived back in Brazil having returned to Europe between races.

Vasseur said on Friday: "It went well. It was good to discuss. It was good to clarify our positions and now we turn the page.

"The guidelines are still the same. They need to respect each other. They are competitive with fighting spirit but they need to respect the other one and the brand and the people working back home and on track.

"The message was clear and will stay clear. Overall it is true that they are working for the team and the team has to come first. It's clear we failed and we have to react but the meeting was a clear reminder that Ferrari comes first."

The magnitude of this situation is obvious, as is the difficulty in finding a solution, and the potential for further trouble down the line.

Hamilton has been especially outspoken on this topic.

The seven-time champion has drawn a contrast between the way Leclerc races him and the way he approaches other drivers, pointing to him ceding to Max Verstappen when they were racing side by side to the first corner in Singapore, compared with how he dealt with Hamilton in Mexico City.

"We could have easily had a one-two and so we definitely have to work towards making sure that doesn't happen again," Hamilton said, adding that he thought this was a theme between Leclerc and his team-mates that he had also seen with his predecessors Sebastian Vettel and Carlos Sainz.

He also said: "Of course, there's some times you say things and maybe you might regret it afterwards, but I don't.

"I've never apologised for being authentic and real. And I'm not going to be silenced. I have not been asked to not say anything. And that's just the way it is.

"I wear my heart on my sleeve and I say how I feel in the moment."

From Vasseur's point of view, this is a problem that really needs to be solved because if Ferrari can keep hold of the chassis advantage they have had this year and bring their engine up to the level of Mercedes and Red Bull, they could be title contenders next year.

Hamilton said: "Naturally, it's not so easy having someone like me come into a team because I'm very outspoken and I push and push and push, push for so many changes and I'm going to be pushing for more.

"As long as I'm here, that's how it's going to be. I'm here to win. And to be able to win, you have to work with everyone around you.

"I truly believe that this team can be fighting for the championship next year.

"I'm in the process of working with the head of aero, the head of aerodynamics to make sure that we hold on to the goodness of the car we have this year and fix some of the small, subtle things that could be better.

"And obviously, the power-unit, they're doing their thing and I really hope that they're able to pull through."

At Red Bull, the situation is much simpler as the team build serious momentum in this final part of the season.

Verstappen was the beneficiary of the Ferrari battle in Mexico, and his victory there was his third in four races.

That has moved him up into second in the drivers' championship - something that looked impossible as the team floundered in the first third of the year, when they were not far off a second off the pace.

"It's a big surprise to be second in the championship, but we take it," Verstappen said.

"We had a lot of difficulties as a team in the beginning. The car was not where we wanted it to be. Probably also we still had to learn quite a bit from the power units, and I think we really learned a lot throughout the season.

"From my side, it's just you never really give up or, in terms of, like, you just never really settle for P6 or P7, right?

"Even when I was in that position or fighting the midfield, I was still trying to do the best that I could get out of the situation.

"Sometimes that is a P6 when the car is not able to perform better. But then once the car is in a better window, then you can fight further up front and eventually, of course, win races.…

Alan Jones, the last Australian and first Williams driver to win the Formula 1 world title, has died at the age of 80.

Jones raced in F1 between 1975 and 1986, winning the title in 1980 to become the first of Williams' seven world champions.

Jones, who turned 80 on Monday, won 12 grands prix in his career and raced competitively in other formats until 2002.

"We are extremely saddened to announce the passing of our beloved Alan, who passed away on 5 November following a short illness," his wife Amanda Butler-Davis said in a statement released on her behalf by Motorsport Australia.

"He will be dearly missed and fondly remembered by those closest to him, as well as the many fans whose support he was always grateful for."

Jones started the first of his 116 F1 races in a Hesketh at the 1975 Spanish Grand Prix.

He won his first race for the Shadow team in Austria in 1977 before joining Williams the following year.

After finishing third in the drivers' championship in 1979, he won five races in 1980 and finished on the podium in all but one of the grands prix he completed, taking the title ahead of Nelson Piquet.

Jones was the second Australian to win the F1 championship, after Jack Brabham in 1959, 1960 and 1966.

Jones remains the most recent Australian to triumph at the Australian Grand Prix, winning at Melbourne's Calder Park Raceway in 1980 when the race was not part of the world championship.

He finished third in the drivers' standings in 1981, winning in Las Vegas for what proved to be his final race victory. He retired at the end of the season.

Having appeared in one race for Arrows in 1983, Jones made a full-time comeback with new team Haas in 1985 and raced largely unsuccessfully the following year.

He continued to compete in touring car and endurance races, mostly in Australia, and became a popular motorsports pundit on television in his home country.

"Alan dedicated his life to motorsport, building a legacy that will live on through the countless people he touched along the way," Butler-Davis said.

"Through his achievements, passion and unmistakable character, both on and off the track, Alan left an enduring mark on the sport both nationally and across the globe."

Alan Jones' time at the very peak of F1 was short - essentially just under three years from mid-1979 to the end of 1981 - but he left a lasting impression.

Jones is synonymous with the Williams team, having become their first world champion in 1980, and he formed a close, almost brotherly bond with co-founders Frank Williams and Patrick Head.

Williams and Head loved Jones' pugnacious, no-nonsense approach, and between them they were the leading force in F1 for a short time, as the team first emerged at the forefront of the sport.

Future Williams drivers, whoever they were, were almost always measured against Jones, and usually came up wanting in Williams' and Head's eyes.

After making his debut, it took a little while for Jones' abilities to be appreciated. But victory for the unfancied Shadow team in the 1977 Austrian Grand Prix, beating Niki Lauda's Ferrari fair and square, was an indicator of his potential.

Moving to Williams in 1978, the team showed well with their neat FW06 design, the first led by Head at the start of his iconic career.

But it was 1979 when Jones and Williams really turned it on. When the new FW07 car debuted mid-season, it and Jones soon became the standard setters.

Early reliability problems meant he was unable to challenge Ferrari drivers Jody Scheckter and Gilles Villeneuve for the title under the season's bizarre split scoring system, but he won four of the final six races to set the tone for the following year.

In 1980, with the upgraded FW07B, Jones and Williams were the team to beat. Pushed hard to the title by Brabham's Nelson Piquet, for whom Jones had little time, he won five of the 14 races and clinched the title with a race to spare.

He could and arguably should have won again in 1981, but a couple of retirements and some errors restricted his victory tally to the first and last grands prix.

A dominant victory on the unloved new circuit in the Caesars Palace car park in Las Vegas was overshadowed by team-mate Carlos Reutemann's mysterious capitulation in the championship fight with Piquet .

After it, although at the height of his powers, Jones retired at the age of 34, to return to his beloved Australia.

He thought it was the right move, but he soon got the itch to return. A one-off outing for Arrows in 1983 was followed by a full-time comeback for the new US-based Haas team - no relation to the current one of the same name.

But the project was not a success. The car did not debut until the 12th race of 1985, and in 1986 was unreliable and slow, despite help from a then unknown Adrian Newey.

It collapsed at the end of the season, and Jones left F1 for good. He continued to race intermittently into his 50s, and also spent time as an F1 driver steward.

Formula 1's next engine regulations are set to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines that are simplified and less expensive to make compared to the existing rules.

A proposal document sent by governing body the FIA to the six manufacturers in F1 outlines a framework for discussions on engines to be introduced in either 2030 or 2031.

Multiple sources within F1 have provided BBC Sport with the details within the document.

The plan, which comes after initial discussions with individual engine manufacturers on a one-to-one basis, proposes cheaper, lighter, simpler engines with a more visceral sound.

However, the FIA has moved away from its initial proposal to return to naturally aspirated engines.

The stated aim of the new rules is to introduce lighter, more responsive cars, increased emphasis on driver skill, relevant technologies, reduced cost, to make it easier for new manufacturers to enter F1 and to continue with the sport's commitment to reducing emissions.

This comes after criticism of the new engines introduced this year for their complexity and the way their design and operation has diminished the driving challenge of some of F1's best corners.

Will F1 go back to the future with its engines?

The engines used in F1 at the moment are 1.6-litre V6 turbos with a power split of 53-47 between the internal combustion engine and electrical components. This will be changed to 60-40 in two steps by 2028.

The FIA document proposes a V8 engine with a capacity of between 2-2.3-litres with a smaller turbo running at reduced boost pressure and a less powerful hybrid system.

The electrical motor would have a recovery capacity of 200kW compared to the current 350kW.

The idea is for 100kW (134bhp) of this to be available at all times, with a further 100kW to be used for a push-to-pass or overtake mode.

The rest of the total power output of in the region of 900bhp will be provided by the internal combustion engine.

F1 will continue with fully sustainable fuels but with the ambition to make the requirements around them less complex and therefore lower production costs.

The aim is to cut a total of 80kg from the overall weight of the cars.

The proposal changes the previous stance of the FIA on naturally aspirated engines - president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially proposed a return of V10s at the start of last year and has more recently been pushing V8s.

The addition of the turbo satisfies the need for the engines to be road-relevant, as well as increasing efficiency and requiring less fuel than a pure naturally aspirated engine.

The published proposals can be seen as a kind of middle ground between Ben Sulayem's initial stance, the desire of at least some manufacturers to keep turbos and a significant hybrid element, and a recognition that the latest rules were flawed in concept and execution.

The new engines will have none of the problems of energy starvation about which drivers have complained this season.

Fernando Alonso has called F1 the "battery world championship" and described fast corners as "the charging station for the car", while Max Verstappen has described the new rules as "Formula E on steroids" and anti-racing.

Both have since tempered their criticisms having seen that the sport's bosses have listened to their comments on the engines and made immediate changes to the rules this year as well as started working towards a new direction in the future.

The fundamental framework of the proposal for the new engine's architecture is said to be basically acceptable to all the manufacturers.

However, the details around how the rules operate will need discussion.

The document outlines two possible ways forward for the new rule set.

One is aimed at minimising necessary adaptation - for example, a 2.1-litre V8 could be produced by simply adding two cylinders to the current 1.6-litre blocks and reducing the size of the turbo and MGU-K (hybrid motor).

The other, more controversial, is to have an external manufacturer design and supply a baseline power-unit with a high degree of standardisation, on to which manufacturers could add a degree of customisation.

However, insiders say the manufacturers are all aligned on wanting to design and build their own power-units and for engines to remain a performance differentiator.

The companies who currently supply engines to F1 teams are Mercedes, Ferrari, Audi, Honda and Red Bull. Cadillac, which entered F1 this year with its own team, is planning to produce an engine to the new rules.

There are two further arguments to steer away from the standardisation route:

The first is that the reasons for it - to safeguard against manufacturers leaving the sport - is irrelevant as all six will be committed under the new rule set.

The second is that the standardisation of electronics control units this season has led to a series of problems, such as at the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia when cars were restricted to not much more than walking pace because of a software bug.

The document outlines a proposal to cut the engine budget cap by 50% from the current level of $190m (£143m) per year.

However, this is considered a starting point for discussions, while there are also concerns about providing a suitable glide path down to the new number to enable teams to manage the impact on workforces.

Discussions around the budget cap also involve the need to balance ongoing development of the existing engines with design and construction of the new ones.

That topic is interlinked with whether the new rules will come into force in 2030 or 2031.

The existing contracts in F1 bind the FIA, teams and commercial rights holder together only until 2030.

Ben Sulayem has previously threatened to introduce his own rules unilaterally in 2031.

That threat appears to have receded and the process has been marked by a spirit of co-operation, which is expected to continue.…

Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement.

Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time.

But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017.

Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed.

That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work.

Morocco never found the finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town.

For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with.

The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub.

At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.

The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.

But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership.

"It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision".

"Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past.

"It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity."

Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A

From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed.

He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped.

And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal.

Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka.

The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change.

President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa.

Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return.

"We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events."

Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that the project is using money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.

Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion.

The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation.

But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.

The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia.

Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo , at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.

F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda.

Saudi Arabia will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034. Boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi Arabian finance. Golf came close to being torn apart by Saudi money and the establishment of the rival LIV tour.…

For the second time this week, the Yankees have lost a significant member of their coaching staff. Tanner Swanson, the organization’s director of catching since 2020, has been hired by the Seattle Mariners to join new manager Jason Kanzler as their bench coach according to the New York Post’s Joel Sherman . This comes on the heels of Triple-A manager Shelley Duncan defecting over to the Red Sox on Wednesday to join their staff, and now despite not making any firings of their own on the coaching staff the Yankees will have some holes to fill.

Swanson was revolutionary in the organization for developing the team’s ability to frame pitches. Austin Wells has become the model for his work, becoming one of the best pitch framers in the game, and his development lined up directly with Swanson’s arrival in New York. The Yankees have been providing catchers to several teams over the years though, as they traded from their surplus of catchers sending Carlos Narváez over to Boston for Elmer Rodriguez, flipping Jose Trevino to Cincinnati for Fernando Cruz, and including Kyle Higashioka in the package to San Diego that netted Juan Soto.

The loss of Swanson is a big one for the Yankees to swallow, but they’ve hopefully learned enough from his time here to continue the catching pipeline that has netted them so much value. For Swanson, the chance to coach in the major leagues is an opportunity that he couldn’t pass up on, and he’ll now get to work with a premier catcher in Cal Raleigh coming off what was a disappointing follow-up to his MVP runner-up 2025.

The erratic and increasingly injury-prone righty may or may not be on the roster past Nov. 20th.

In 2024, New York Yankees right-hander Luis Gil impressed with a brilliant first half and a full campaign worthy of the American League Rookie of the Year Award. At that point, the Bombers thought they had unearthed another pitching gem, controllable for multiple years on the cheap.

A severe lat strain in 2025 and shoulder issues in 2026 have hampered his progress and affected his fastball velocity and command, though. Last year, he posted a 3.32 ERA in 57 innings, but with very ugly peripherals. This season, the wheels completely fell off. The shoulder woes limited him to 39.1 innings between the majors and the minors. He finished with a 4.61 ERA and a rough 7.12 FIP in 27.1 MLB frames, with 18 walks and 17 strikeouts.

The right-hander started to transition to a bullpen role during the season, which could actually represent his firmest, most concrete way into the team’s plans. With the non-tender deadline looming on November 20th, however, the Yankees will have to make a decision. Is holding onto Gil worth the headache? The right-hander is projected to get a modest raise in his first year of arbitration, to $2.3 million, according to MLB Trade Rumors . Money, in this case, is not the primary issue, though.

Is Gil good or promising enough to warrant a place in the team’s future plans? Well, it will entirely depend on his ability to thrive out of the bullpen, which could be both his short and long-term home.

The concept of Gil as a multi-inning reliever is certainly enticing. Potentially increased velocity and not as much wear and tear on his shoulder sound excellent for his long-term prospects, but he does have short-term goals: looking good on the mound and getting closer to that 2024 version of himself, regardless of role. He was a completely different pitcher back then:

He is currently pitching for Tigres Del Licey in the Dominican Republic League, and boasts a solid 1.50 ERA in six frames, spanning over three games. The problem? He has issued six walks against seven strikeouts. Control has never been Gil’s calling card, but anything that starts with a five next to his BB/9 stat would represent a big problem.

The Yankees would probably love to trade Gil, hoping to get something in return for his name value and the fact that he won the award for the league’s best rookie just two years ago. They are probably dangling his name in the market as we speak. If they can’t reach a deal with any team, they will need to make a decision. They can give their promising, yet erratic right-hander one last chance, probably in the bullpen, or they could choose to cut ties and not tender him a contract, making him free to sign with any squad.

Complicating matters is the fact that Gil does not have any minor league options remaining. The next time the Yankees want to remove him from their 40-man roster, they will need to put him through waivers and risk losing him for nothing. If the Yankees can’t find a deal for him, they could opt to keep him around and try the bullpen experiment full-time to see if he can give them anything there, considering that it’s an area of need at the moment. It’s hard to see him sticking over the long term unless something drastically changes, though.

After the 2018 season, the Yankees’ pitching staff looked thin. Young ace Luis Severino gave them a top-flight starter atop the rotation, and Masahiro Tanaka was a more-than-capable No. 3 starter with a tendency of stepping up in big spots, but Sonny Gray and Domingo Germán were disasters while CC Sabathia and J.A. Happ were on the wrong side of 45. Compared to the Boston Red Sox — led by Chris Sale, Nathan Eovaldi, and David Price — and the three-headed monster of Justin Verlander, Gerrit Cole, and Dallas Keuchel in Houston, it was clear that the Bombers had a lot of catching up to do in the arms race.

To that end, the Yankees opened the 2018-2019 offseason by swinging a deal for James Paxton, sending a package centered on top pitching prospect Justus Sheffield to the Seattle Mariners.

James Alston Paxton Born: November 6, 1988 (Richmond, British Columbia, Canada) Yankees Tenure: 2019-20

Born and raised in British Columbia, Paxton made a name for himself on the Canadian youth baseball circuit, ultimately helping to lead Team Canada to a bronze medal at the 2006 World Junior Baseball Championship. Following his high school career, the Big Maple took his talents to the United States, joining the University of Kentucky. Between his performance with the Wildcats (first as a reliever, then as a starter) and with the summer Alaska Baseball League, he quickly found himself on the radar of Major League ballclubs.

After a junior year in which he struck out 115 batters in 78.1 innings, he was drafted by the Toronto Blue Jays with the 37th overall pick of the 2009 draft (the compensation Toronto received when the Yankees signed A.J. Burnett). Unfortunately, they were unable to come a deal, and Paxton opted to return to Kentucky for his senior year… that is, until the Blue Jays told the media that they had been negotiating with Scott Boras, not with Paxton’s family. Back in the pre-NIL days, hiring an agent changed your status from an amateur to a pro, and he was declared ineligible; an attempt to sue in order to be reinstated led nowhere, and eventually, Paxton withdrew from Kentucky to begin his professional career.

Paxton spent the 2010 season with the Grand Prairie AirHogs, an American Association team which allowed him to retain draft eligibility. On the back of a solid, albeit unspectacular, performance there, he was selected by the Seattle Mariners in the fourth round of the 2010 draft. After a lengthy negotiation, he finally put pen to paper in March 2011, and began what would be a rapid ascent through the minor leagues. He reached Double-A by the end of 2011, received an invitation to spring training in 2012, and finally made his Major League debut on September 7, 2013.

Thanks to a strong cup of coffee in 2013, Paxton began the 2014 season in the Seattle rotation, where he would spend the next five seasons. Unfortunately, he fell into a rather predictable pattern. When healthy, he was one of the league’s premier pitchers: his 13.2 fWAR from 2014 to 2018 ranked 26th out of the 88 starters who went at least 550 innings, and his 18.8 K-BB% ranked 14th — just one-tenth of a percentage point behind Cole and three-tenths behind Tanaka. And on May 8, 2018, he became just the second Canadian-born pitcher to throw a no-hitter in baseball history — a testament to his ability.

However, Paxton was hardly healthy for a full season: he made more than 20 starts just twice in that span, having hit the IL with a lat strain in 2014, a strained tendon in his finger in 2015, a forearm strain and a pec strain in 2017, and back inflammation and a forearm strain in 2018.

When the Yankees acquired Paxton that winter, they gambled that his ability on the mound would be worth the risk of his lengthy injury history. In 2019, that was absolutely the case. In the year where pretty much every member of the Yankees spent time on the injured list, the oft-injured pitcher put together the healthiest season of his career, making 29 starts and spending just a few weeks of May on the shelf.

Despite a nasty tendency to surrender home runs in the first inning, Paxton anchored the Yankees rotation, and when the Yankees needed him most in October, he delivered. Getting the ball with the team down 3-1 in the ALCS and having dropped three consecutive games, Paxton shook off two less-than-stellar postseason starts to shut down the Astros lineup, striking out nine and allowing just one run in six innings to send the series back to Houston. Sure, things didn’t get any better from there, but that’s another story (and not any of Paxton’s fault, either).

As good as things went for Paxton in 2019, however, that’s how bad 2020 went. On February 5th, he underwent lumbar surgery, which would have sidelined him for 3-4 months if the season hadn’t been delayed because of the pandemic. Although he made it back in time for the late-July Opening Day, he put together the worst season of his career, posting a 6.64 ERA in 20.1 innings across five starts before hitting the shelf again, this time with a left flexor tendon strain — perhaps the reason for the diminished velocity that made him suddenly very hittable.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the Yankees opted to let Paxton walk in free agency, and he returned to the Seattle Mariners on a one-year deal. After just 1.1 innings, though, he left the game with an elbow injury, and later that week, it was announced that he needed Tommy John surgery.…

Fernando Cruz was having a solid campaign before a partial UCL tear brought his 2026 season to an end.

One of the most beautiful parts of baseball is how many different personal journeys we fans get to learn about as players chase their dreams. Fernando Cruz’s story aside, let’s dive into the season that earned him a B- from the staff here at Pinstripe Alley.

Cruz’s 2026 really started at the World Baseball Classic, representing Team Puerto Rico. After rejoining the Yankees, he picked up where he left off last season as a trusted member of Aaron Boone’s bullpen. From there, it became a story of two halves.

2026 Stats: 61 games, 54.2 IP, 3.13 ERA (135 ERA+), 4.17 FIP, 4.39 xFIP, 28.6 K%, 13.7 BB%, 0.0 fWAR, 1.2 rWAR, 4-6 record

2027 Contract Status: Arbitration-eligible

Before the All-Star break, Cruz was excellent. He was a borderline All-Star, striking out 50 batters over 40 innings while holding opponents to a .191 batting average. His best month of the season was May, when he appeared in 14 games and posted a 1.02 WHIP while allowing just two earned runs over 13.2 innings. He was one of the more dependable pieces out of the bullpen during the first half of what was an underrated unit.

The key to this effectiveness was his splitter, which he deployed 51.3 percent of the time. He paired that pitch with a four-seamer, sweeper, and sinker to keep hitters off-balance. The splitter continued to be his best weapon, generating a 52 percent whiff rate and limiting hitters to a .161 average against it.

After the break, however, his performance began to slip. Something seemed off as Cruz started losing some control in late July, and August became his roughest month of the season. He posted a 6.75 ERA over eight innings, allowing six home runs and four walks. Following a blown save against Houston on August 25th, the Yankees announced that Cruz had suffered a partial tear of his right ulnar collateral ligament, and he landed on the injured list the following day.

The ultimate team guy, Cruz opted to pursue a non-surgical approach after receiving a second opinion with the hope he could make it back in 2026. He received a cortisone shot and started rehabbing trying to find his way back into the mix for the postseason. However, a month after landing on the injured list, the Yankees transferred Cruz to the 60-day injured list on September 25th, ending his chances of returning during the 2026 season.

On the season, Cruz had some impressive underlying numbers. He ranked in the 91st percentile in average exit velocity and the 99th percentile in whiff rate. He also landed in the 82nd percentile in xERA, the 88th percentile in strikeout rate, and the 85th percentile in extension. However, his hard-hit rate ranked in just the 22nd percentile, and his walk rate was in the third percentile. The right-hander was also effective against left-handed hitters holding them to a .180 batting average.

Losing Cruz after the Trade Deadline was less than ideal, especially with the Yankees having few options capable of replacing his production internally, which led to the Michael Fulmer experience. As the page turns to a new season, with the injury question mark hovering over him, Cruz becomes an interesting offseason decision for the Yankees.

The team has until November 20th to tender him a contract for the 2027 season. Depending on the outlook for his elbow, it would not surprise me to see the Yankees retain him and try to work out a deal before arbitration. Given the injury uncertainty, it could be a buy-low opportunity for the club, provided they believe he can return to form and he is willing to accept a similar salary to last season. However, professional baseball is a business and the team might opt to use the money and roster spot they would spend on Cruz elsewhere this offseason.

Personally, I gave Cruz a B for this season, and in hindsight, I feel that might have been a touch low. What grade would you assign Cruz, and what are your thoughts on him in pinstripes in 2027?
